The risky condition can be created in one place, carried through several branches or calls, and exposed only when a later operation uses it badly. A sequence model, meaning a model that reads code mostly in written order, can notice local patterns such as a familiar function name near a buffer, but the real dependency may jump across the file. A graph model improves this by representing abstract syntax trees and control flow graphs, where nodes are code pieces and links show syntactic nesting or possible execution movement. The abstract says those graph methods still often rely on shallow code features. That means they may know that two nodes are connected without understanding what the operations at those nodes mean. The central tension is structure versus meaning: the model needs the route through the code and the semantic content of the code on that route.
953.naive: A smart beginner would first collect many C files labeled vulnerable or safe, turn each file into a stream of words and symbols, and train a classifier to recognize repeated bad-looking patterns. That can work for obvious cases where the dangerous call and its unsafe argument sit close together. It fails when the danger depends on a non-linear relationship: a value is checked on one branch but not another, or a later operation depends on a condition far away. The next beginner move would be to build AST and CFG graphs and classify from simple graph features. The abstract says that still falls short when those features are shallow, because a structural edge alone does not explain the meaning of the operation it connects.
953.ap: The core move is to build a code representation that keeps three kinds of evidence at once. First, the program is represented as graphs, including syntax structure and control flow, so the model can see relationships that are not adjacent in the written text. Second, Graph Attention Networks are used to decide which neighboring graph nodes deserve more influence, instead of treating every link as equally informative. Third, Restricted Boltzmann Machines are jointly trained with the graph attention part to mine hidden feature patterns from the code graphs. The paper then adds node-level semantic information from code language models, meaning models trained to read code and produce useful descriptions of what each code piece does. These structural and semantic signals are fused into node representations. Finally, a hybrid loss trains the system both to detect vulnerabilities and to track paths, so localization is part of learning rather than an afterthought.
953.mech: The input is a C program that can be broken into graph nodes and graph links. A node may stand for a code element, while links come from structures such as an abstract syntax tree, which records how code pieces are nested, and a control flow graph, which records which execution steps can follow which. The first transformation is structural: a Graph Attention Network passes information between linked nodes, but weights the incoming messages so that more relevant neighbors matter more for the current node. In parallel or joint training, a Restricted Boltzmann Machine searches for hidden regularities in the graph-derived features. In plain terms, it tries to discover combinations of structural clues that often appear together even when they were not directly labeled by a human. The second transformation is semantic: a code language model produces node-level meaning signals, so a node is not represented only by its graph position but also by what its code operation appears to do. These structural and semantic signals are fused into fuller node representations. During training, a Graph Transformer models long-range dependencies across the whole code graph, letting distant but related nodes affect one another. The output is a vulnerability decision, and the hybrid training objective also pushes the model to identify path context so the warning can be localized along relevant program paths.
953.math: The main mathematical object is a graph: code parts become nodes, and program relationships become edges. Graph reasoning fits because the question is not only what symbols appear, but how evidence should travel through syntax and execution links. Attention, unpacked here as weighted listening, asks each node which connected nodes should influence it most. That is a scoring problem: every neighbor receives a learned weight, and the node updates itself more from high-weight neighbors than from low-weight ones. The Restricted Boltzmann Machine adds another idea: hidden-variable learning. It keeps visible features from the graph and learns hidden switches that explain recurring combinations among them, without needing every such combination to be manually named. The code language model supplies learned semantic features, meaning numeric summaries of code meaning learned from many examples of code. The Graph Transformer extends weighted listening beyond immediate neighbors, so far-apart nodes can still exchange evidence when the graph suggests a program-wide dependency. The hybrid loss is the rule for what counts as wrong: wrong vulnerability labels are penalized, and poor path tracking is also penalized. The tradeoff is richer context versus false confidence: combining many signals can reveal subtle bugs, but it can also overtrust patterns that only look meaningful in the training data.
953.dots: This paper sits where graph learning, security, language models, and explanation meet. It shares the graph-learning idea that isolated records are too thin: a code node becomes clearer when its neighbors, control paths, and distant dependencies are considered. It shares the language-model idea that raw symbols need meaning, because the same structural shape can be safe or unsafe depending on what the operations do. It also connects to privacy and security work in the broader conference through the practical pressure of detecting attacks before deployment, though here the protected object is source code rather than private user records. The path-tracking objective links it to explainability: a detector that only says vulnerable gives less help than one that indicates the route through the code that made the decision plausible. Compared with generic ranking or retrieval papers, the scoring here is not about choosing documents for a user. It is about sorting code behavior into safe, risky, and traceable evidence paths.
953.ww: The approach should improve over the naive sequence reader because it matches the shape of the object being studied. A C program is not a flat sentence. It is a set of nested expressions, possible execution routes, and long-distance dependencies. If a vulnerable behavior is created by a path through the program, then a graph gives the detector a better map of where evidence can travel. The attention weights help because not every neighbor is equally useful; a syntax parent, a control successor, and a distant node may carry different amounts of security evidence. The RBM part helps if recurring hidden graph patterns mark vulnerable code even when the surface syntax varies. The code language model helps because structure alone cannot tell whether an operation is a harmless assignment or a risky memory use. The hybrid loss helps by making localization part of the objective: the model is rewarded for learning the path context behind the label, so it is less likely to treat detection as a single unexplained file-level guess.
953.po: The payoff is a detector that combines code structure, code meaning, and path-aware training rather than relying on one view of the program. According to the abstract, Vul-GRT is evaluated on the NVD and SARD vulnerability datasets and is reported to outperform existing methods in effectiveness and robustness. The practical gain is not just a stronger yes-or-no vulnerability classifier. Because the method includes path tracking during training, it aims to make flagged vulnerabilities more traceable, which matters to developers who need to inspect and fix the risky code path rather than merely receive an alarm.
953.limits: The abstract supports the overall mechanism but leaves several assumptions open. The method depends on AST and CFG construction capturing the relationships that matter for real C vulnerabilities; missing or noisy graphs would weaken it. It also assumes the code language model's node-level semantics transfer to the vulnerable code being tested. The NVD and SARD experiments show evidence on two datasets, but the abstract does not prove performance on every project style, compiler setting, or newly invented attack pattern. More components also mean more places for error: attention weights, hidden features, semantic features, and path objectives must reinforce one another rather than amplify misleading training shortcuts.

954.bp: This paper serves the ordinary problem behind a movie recommender: a service must choose a short list for people it knows well and for people it barely knows at all. Those are different situations. A warm-start user has a trail of ratings or interactions, so the system can compare that user with past choices. A cold-start user arrives with little history, so the usual behavior-based evidence is thin. MARS treats recommendation as a routing problem before it treats it as a ranking problem. A central manager looks at the user context and decides which specialist should handle the request. Established users go to Bayesian Personalized Ranking, a model built to learn which movies a user should prefer over other movies from past behavior. New users go to Sentence-BERT semantic search, which compares movie meaning through language rather than through the user's own history. The paper is about when precision and discovery cannot both be maximized by one path.
954.wh: The hard part is that the system is asked to serve two unlike needs with one interface. For warm-start users, the practical goal is precision: show movies that match a known taste record. For cold-start users, the record is missing, so precision measured against past preference is naturally weak. A popularity rule can look good because many users like popular movies, but it mostly repeats safe choices. The abstract's numbers make that tension explicit: for cold-start users, popularity has much higher precision than the MARS semantic path, while the semantic path has far higher novelty. That means the system is not merely choosing a better model; it is choosing which kind of failure it is willing to accept. A single recommender can hide this difference by averaging across users. It may look strong for established users while quietly giving new users either stale popular items or adventurous suggestions that are harder to verify as immediately right.
954.naive: A smart beginner would build one recommender and send every user through it. The simplest version would rank movies by popularity, because popularity works even when a new user has no history. A slightly more advanced version would use one behavior-based ranking model for everyone, trusting it to learn from the MovieLens record. Both choices break at the boundary between known and unknown users. Popularity gives new users safe hits, but it has little reason to surface movies outside the obvious pile. A behavior-based model can be strong for warm-start users, but for cold-start users it has too little personal evidence to know which comparisons matter. The result is either precise but unsurprising lists, or personalized machinery pointed at users for whom personalization evidence has not yet arrived.
954.ap: The core idea is to make the first decision a managerial one: ask what kind of evidence exists for this user, then choose the recommendation path that fits that evidence. MARS uses a Manager Agent as a dispatcher. If the user is established, the manager sends the request to the Bayesian Personalized Ranking path, which is designed to order movies by learned user preference. If the user is new, the manager sends the request to a semantic search path based on Sentence-BERT, where movie descriptions or related language can be compared even without a deep user history. This is a hybrid system, but the important move is not simply combining two models. It is refusing to pretend that cold-start and warm-start recommendation are the same mathematical problem. The system preserves the strong warm-start behavior of BPR while giving cold-start users a discovery-oriented route that the abstract reports as much faster and much more novel.
954.mech: The mechanism begins with a request from a user who needs recommendations. The first input is not only the candidate movie set; it is the user context, especially whether the user has enough past behavior to be treated as warm-start. The Manager Agent reads that context and chooses one of two paths. On the warm-start path, the request goes to Bayesian Personalized Ranking. In plain terms, BPR learns from past user-item interactions by comparing pairs: for a given user, a movie with positive evidence should be placed above a movie with weaker or missing evidence. Its output is an ordered list shaped by the user's observed history. The paper reports that MARS matches the strong BPR baseline for warm-start users across all metrics, so the routing layer does not appear to damage that established-user path. On the cold-start path, the request goes to Sentence-BERT semantic search. Sentence-BERT turns pieces of language into comparable numeric descriptions, so the system can search by meaning when direct personal behavior is scarce. That path scores candidate movies by semantic closeness rather than by a long user history. The output is still a recommendation list, but it is optimized for a different practical role: discovery. The experiments then compare this routed system with baselines on MovieLens 20M, measuring precision, novelty, and latency.
954.math: The mathematical ideas are ranking, similarity, probability-shaped preference learning, and routing under a tradeoff. Ranking is the act of turning many possible movies into an order, because the service can show only a few. BPR gives ranking a pairwise form: instead of asking for an absolute score for every movie, it learns that one movie should stand above another for a user when past behavior supports that comparison. The word Bayesian signals that uncertainty is part of the language: user preference is not directly observed as a complete truth, so the model infers a likely ordering from partial interactions. Sentence-BERT uses similarity. It compresses language about items into numeric descriptions and then asks which descriptions are close. That compression loses detail, but it makes search possible when a user has little behavior history. The manager adds a decision rule over these mathematical tools: choose pairwise preference ranking when personal evidence exists, and choose semantic closeness when it does not. The central tradeoff is precision versus discovery. Precision rewards matching known or expected preferences; discovery rewards surfacing less obvious items. The abstract's cold-start results show these goals separating rather than collapsing into one score.
954.dots: This paper sits inside the recommender-systems family described in the repo: systems must choose a small set of useful items from a huge pile while user intent, item meaning, cost, and feedback all move. It connects directly to ranking because both BPR and the final output are ordered choices under limited attention. It connects to similarity because the cold-start path uses language-based closeness when behavior-based comparison is weak. It also connects to probability, since warm-start recommendation estimates preference from partial repeated evidence rather than reading a user's true taste directly. Within the same WSDM batch, MOCHA also handles recommendation by selecting relevant item and feature knowledge for conversational recommendations, while EFMRec handles missing item modalities by using available evidence and ignoring absent evidence. MARS has the same deeper shape: do not force every request through one evidence channel. Route or combine evidence according to what is actually present.
954.ww: The design works when the user-context split captures a real difference in evidence quality. Warm-start users have enough history for BPR's pairwise comparisons to be meaningful. In that setting, replacing the ranking model would risk throwing away the strongest signal, so MARS keeps the proven BPR path and only wraps it with orchestration. That explains why the abstract emphasizes matching the strong BPR baseline for warm-start users. Cold-start users have the opposite problem: their behavior trail is too short for personal ranking to have much grip. Semantic search can still act because item language exists before the user has a long record. It can move through movie meaning rather than through user-specific history, which makes it better suited for finding unfamiliar or less common items. The reason precision drops is also the reason novelty rises: the semantic path is less anchored to what many users already chose. The speed result follows from the same separation if the cold-start semantic path avoids heavier personalized ranking work for users whose history would not justify it.
954.po: The payoff is an adaptive recommender architecture with a measurable tradeoff instead of a hidden compromise. For established users, MARS keeps the warm-start performance of the strong BPR baseline across the reported metrics. For new users, it exposes the cost of discovery clearly: popularity wins on precision, but the MARS semantic path delivers over ten times higher novelty and is reported as more than twenty times faster. That gives system builders a concrete design choice. If the goal for a new user is safe immediate accuracy, popularity may be appropriate. If the goal is fast exploration beyond obvious movies, the semantic path buys that capability.
954.limits: The claims depend on the user split being reliable: the manager must correctly identify when a user is warm-start or cold-start, and those categories must correspond to different evidence needs. The abstract reports MovieLens 20M experiments, so it does not prove the same precision-discovery balance for other item domains, richer user profiles, or live feedback loops. Novelty is useful only if users value discovery rather than just familiar hits. The semantic path also assumes movie language captures meaningful item relationships. The abstract gives latency, precision, and novelty evidence, but not long-term satisfaction, retention, fairness, or whether users prefer the discovery lists.

955.bp: This paper serves a very practical checking problem: a public post may be false, and it may have been written by a person, by a language model, or by both. That source matters because the surface clues differ. Human-written falsehoods may be clumsy, emotional, or locally inconsistent, while language-model falsehoods can be fluent, confident, and persuasive even when they are unsupported. A veracity system therefore cannot only ask whether the wording looks suspicious. It also has to ask what outside evidence is needed to judge the post. Some posts may be easy enough to judge from their own content. Others need a small amount of retrieved evidence. Others need more checking because their polish hides the missing support. MoARE treats fact checking as an evidence-budgeting problem: for each post, decide whether to retrieve evidence and how much evidence is worth the time.
955.wh: The hard part is that the system does not know the generation source in advance, yet the source changes what kind of checking is useful. If every post gets the same retrieval treatment, the system wastes time on easy cases and under-checks hard ones. Pulling no evidence is fast but risky, because a fluent false claim can look reasonable in isolation. Pulling a large evidence set for every post is safer in spirit, but it is slow and can bring in irrelevant material that distracts the judgment. The abstract also points to a second difficulty: current adaptive retrieval methods mostly react to general difficulty or model confidence. That misses a more specific pattern, namely that human and language-model text can need different evidence depth even when both look readable. The central tension is accuracy versus time cost under hidden source differences.
955.naive: A smart beginner would attach one retrieval-augmented checker to all posts. The checker would fetch a fixed number of documents, feed them with the post into a language model, and ask for a true-or-false judgment. This is sensible because false claims often need outside evidence. It fails because the fixed rule treats unlike cases alike. A short human rumor, a polished language-model fabrication, and a mixed post with partial truth may not need the same number of sources. The beginner might then add a confidence threshold: retrieve more when the model is unsure. That still misses the paper's concern, because fluent generated falsehoods can create false confidence while needing targeted evidence.
955.ap: The core idea is to replace one uniform retrieval habit with a small team of specialized retrieval behaviors. MoARE, a mixture of adaptive retrieval experts, lets different experts represent different ways of spending evidence: perhaps no retrieval, light retrieval, or heavier retrieval, depending on the post. A gating network chooses among these experts for each input without being told whether the post came from a human or a language model. The training signal rewards two things at once: judging veracity correctly and avoiding unnecessary time cost. In plain terms, the system learns a policy for spending checking effort. It should spend little effort when the post already carries enough reliable signal, and more effort when outside evidence is likely to change the truth judgment.
955.mech: The input is one post whose truth must be assessed, drawn from a setting where human and language-model generation are mixed. The system first reads the post and forms internal signals about its content. Instead of immediately applying one fixed retrieval setting, it passes those signals to a routing part, the mixture-of-experts network. Each expert corresponds to a retrieval behavior, meaning a different decision about whether to retrieve and how much evidence to retrieve. The router assigns the post to an expert or blends expert choices, producing an action about evidence use. If retrieval is chosen, the system fetches outside evidence for the post; if more evidence is chosen, it spends more time collecting support. The retrieved evidence and the original post are then used for the final veracity assessment. During training, reinforcement learning, which means learning by receiving rewards for better actions, adjusts the router and experts. The reward balances two measured outcomes: correct truth judgments and lower time cost. Over many examples, the system learns which post characteristics tend to justify extra evidence and which do not. The output is a veracity decision made with a retrieval amount chosen specifically for that post rather than fixed across the whole dataset.
955.math: The main mathematical object is a decision under uncertainty. For each post, the system must choose an evidence action before knowing for sure how helpful that evidence will be. The mixture-of-experts idea treats the action space as several specialized helpers rather than one average rule. A routing function scores which helper fits the current post. This is a matching problem in miniature: match this post to the retrieval behavior that is likely to be useful. Retrieval itself uses similarity, which means comparing the post to candidate evidence and selecting material judged close enough to help. The reinforcement-learning part adds a reward ledger. A good action receives credit when it improves the truth judgment, but it loses credit when it spends too much time. That makes the tradeoff explicit: accuracy versus cost. The system is not merely minimizing errors in a static label table; it is learning which action should be taken before the final evidence is known. The mathematical fit is natural because the world supplies partial clues. Fluency, semantic pattern, and post content hint at retrieval need, but they do not reveal it perfectly. A learned policy can reuse repeated patterns across posts while still making a per-post choice.
955.dots: This paper sits where three recurring conference ideas meet. From the misinformation and trust family, it inherits the warning that fluent presentation is not the same as verified truth, especially when generated text can be persuasive. From the retrieval-augmented RAG family, it inherits the evidence-selection problem: outside documents can ground a judgment, but too much or poorly chosen evidence adds cost and distraction. From the matching and information concepts in the repo, it asks how scarce checking effort should be assigned. Each post is a candidate case; each retrieval expert is a possible way to spend evidence; the router decides which pairing is worth it. It also connects to ranking and uncertainty because retrieved evidence must be selected and because the system must decide when its current information is not enough. The paper is not just another fake-news classifier; it is an adaptive evidence allocation method for mixed human and language-model content.
955.ww: The mechanism should help because it attacks the main waste in a uniform checker. A fixed retrieval system has to pick one compromise for all posts. If it chooses little retrieval, it misses polished falsehoods that require outside evidence. If it chooses heavy retrieval, it burns time on posts that could have been judged with less support. MoARE gives the system a middle path: learn from many examples which surface and semantic patterns tend to call for which evidence budget. The router does not need an explicit source label, because source differences can leave indirect traces in the post's content and retrieval needs. The reward also prevents a trivial solution where the system always retrieves more. Extra evidence helps only if the accuracy gain is worth the time. That pressure can make the learned behavior sharper: spend checking resources where they are likely to change the decision, and avoid spending them where they mostly repeat what is already clear.
955.po: The payoff is a veracity assessor better suited to a web where false information may be human-written, language-model-written, or mixed. According to the abstract, MoARE improves over retrieval-augmented baselines by achieving higher accuracy with lower time cost on recent mixed-generation datasets. The practical capability is not simply a better label. It is a more economical checking workflow: the system learns when evidence is needed and how much to fetch for each post, without requiring prior knowledge of the post's generation source.
955.limits: The method assumes the training datasets contain enough mixed human and language-model cases for the router to learn useful retrieval patterns. It also assumes retrieved evidence is available, relevant, and not itself misleading. The abstract reports better accuracy and lower time cost, but it does not prove that the learned routing will hold across new topics, languages, platforms, or future language models whose falsehoods have different styles. It also does not show whether attackers can write posts that trigger too little retrieval. The source is hidden by design, so the system's choices need careful auditing before being trusted in high-stakes fact checking.

956.bp: A deployed learning model is often treated like a guarded recipe. The owner spent money collecting data, training the model, and tuning it until it answers useful questions quickly enough for real use. This paper studies a particular kind of recipe, a hyperdimensional computing model, where information is represented by very long patterns of numbers and decisions are made by comparing a new pattern with learned class patterns. The appeal of this style is the balance claimed in the abstract: useful accuracy with efficient computation. That same trained behavior is also intellectual property. The attacker in this paper does not get the recipe, the training examples, or the internal settings. They only get to ask the model questions and see how similar the model thinks each answer is. The practical question is whether repeated questioning can reconstruct a working copy. StealHD says yes, even when the attacker starts with no real data.
956.wh: The hard part is that ordinary model stealing usually leans on at least one crutch. If an attacker has examples from the same world as the training data, they can ask the victim model about those examples and train a copy from the answers. If the attacker can inspect the model, they can use internal structure directly. This paper removes both crutches. The attack is data-free, meaning no original training examples are assumed, and black-box, meaning the attacker sees only query outputs. That leaves a strange search problem: what questions should the attacker ask when they do not know the kinds of inputs the original model learned from? Random questions may land in meaningless parts of the input world and teach the copy little. The abstract's central tension is therefore about making useful fake inputs without data, then using only output similarities to recover behavior rather than exact hidden parameters.
956.naive: A smart beginner might try to query the victim model with arbitrary random inputs, record the returned class or similarity scores, and train another HDC model on that query log. This treats the victim like an oracle that can label unlimited examples. The failure is that unlimited examples are not automatically useful examples. If the queries do not resemble the input patterns that HDC models respond to in a meaningful way, the victim's answers may mostly describe behavior in irrelevant corners of the space. Another beginner might try common data augmentation, making small variations of random seeds, but without knowing which variations matter for HDC, those changes can be noise without structure. The copy would learn many answers, but not necessarily the decision behavior that matters on realistic inputs.
956.ap: StealHD's core move is to exploit the shape of hyperdimensional computing itself rather than the victim's private training set. The abstract says the attack is inspired by characteristics of the HDC algorithm. In concrete terms, the attacker builds a substitute pool of inputs using three noise back-ends and eight augmentations. A noise back-end supplies raw artificial material. An augmentation is a controlled way of changing that material so the generated inputs follow patterns that HDC is likely to treat as meaningful. The attacker then sends these generated inputs to the victim model and observes output similarities, not merely a single hard answer. Those similarities act like richer teaching signals: they say which outputs are close, strong, weak, or ambiguous. A new HDC model is then trained to imitate that behavior, producing a functional copy rather than recovering the exact original internals.
956.mech: The mechanism starts with an attacker who has access to a query interface. The input is any candidate example the attacker chooses; the output is the victim HDC model's similarity response. First, StealHD creates a surrogate dataset, meaning a made-up training set used only for the attack. It does this from three noise back-ends, which can be understood as three ways to produce raw synthetic patterns before any label is known. Second, it applies eight different augmentations, meaning eight systematic transformations of those raw patterns. The abstract does not list the transformations, so the safe claim is only that they are chosen to follow patterns suggested by HDC's behavior. Third, each synthetic input is sent to the victim model. The attacker records the output similarities, which are measurements of how strongly the victim relates the input to possible outputs. Fourth, those query-response pairs become training material for a surrogate HDC model. The copy is adjusted so that, when it sees the synthetic inputs, its own similarity outputs resemble the victim's. The final output is not a stolen parameter file. It is a model with matching function: for relevant inputs, it is intended to answer like the victim.
956.math: The main mathematical idea is function learning from examples. A model can be viewed as a rule that turns an input into an output. If the rule is hidden, repeated input-output observations can still reveal enough of its behavior to train another rule. Here the examples are not real data; they are synthetic queries plus the victim's similarity responses. A second idea is sampling: choosing which parts of a huge possible input world to inspect. Pure random sampling wastes effort if most points teach little, so StealHD shapes the samples with noise sources and augmentations tied to HDC behavior. A third idea is similarity, which means reducing the relation between a new pattern and learned output patterns to scores that can be compared. HDC itself is built around very long numerical patterns, so similarity is a natural language for both decisions and stealing. Training the surrogate is also an error-reduction problem: define the mismatch between victim and copy outputs as wrongness, then change the copy to reduce that mismatch. The tradeoff is practical fidelity versus query and synthetic generation cost.
956.dots: This paper sits in the conference's model stealing attack theme, where the shared problem is that a public prediction interface can leak a private trained behavior. It connects to security papers because the attacker is not trying to corrupt an answer but to copy the useful rule behind many answers. It also connects to learning-from-examples work: the surrogate model is trained in the ordinary supervised way, except the labels or similarity targets come from another model rather than a human or a dataset. There is a link to synthetic-data and augmentation ideas as well. Many papers use generated or transformed data to cover missing cases; here that same idea becomes an attack tool. Finally, it touches efficient learning, because HDC's strength, compact high-dimensional comparison, also gives the attacker a structure to imitate. The broader lesson is that speed and accuracy do not automatically imply protection against query-based copying.
956.ww: The attack should work better than naive querying because it asks questions that are shaped by the victim model's computational language. An HDC model does not treat inputs as isolated names; it maps them into long patterns and makes decisions by comparing those patterns with learned references. If the attacker's generated inputs exercise the comparisons that HDC actually uses, then the victim's similarity outputs reveal more than final class names. They show the copy how the victim ranks possible outputs, which cases are close to boundaries, and which generated variations leave the answer stable. Augmentations help because they create families of related inputs rather than unrelated points. A copy trained on such families can learn not only isolated answers but the local shape of the victim's behavior. The method does not need the original data if HDC's algorithmic characteristics are strong enough to make synthetic query patterns informative. That is the key reason the data-free setting becomes possible rather than hopeless.
956.po: The payoff is a stronger warning about protecting trained HDC models. The abstract reports experiments on three datasets and says StealHD can effectively steal an HDC model under the strict data-free, black-box setting. That means the attack needs only a query channel and observed output similarities, not the owner's data or model parameters. For practitioners, the result says that an efficient HDC deployment may still expose enough behavioral information to be copied. For researchers, it identifies a sharper security test: defenses should consider attackers who manufacture their own query data instead of assuming theft requires access to real training examples.
956.limits: Several assumptions must hold. The attacker must be allowed to send enough queries and receive output similarities rich enough to train from; a system that returns only limited answers might leak less. The synthetic data must also cover behavior that matters for future use, not only artificial cases. The abstract says the method is inspired by HDC characteristics, so the same recipe may not transfer unchanged to models whose input handling is very different. The evidence named here is experimental results on three datasets, but the abstract does not state dataset types, query budgets, exact augmentations, defense settings, or whether the stolen model matches the victim under deployment drift.

957.bp: A news search engine is not just a directory of links. For controversial topics, it becomes one of the ways people learn what their society is arguing about. If a person in one region sees one set of sources, angles, and claims while a person elsewhere sees a different set, both may believe they have sampled the public record even though the system has quietly narrowed the view. This paper studies that narrowing from the end user's side. The real object is a search results page produced by two globally dominant search engines for six controversial topics, observed over two months. The paper asks whether changing only the user's geographic location changes the picture of the issue, whether the two engines behave differently, whether regional events change the bubble over time, and whether some topics are more bubble-prone than others.
957.wh: The hard part is separating real geographic personalization from everything else that can change a search page. Search results vary because engines update their indexes, ranking rules, news freshness signals, and source availability. They can also vary because users differ in language, device, history, account state, or query wording. The abstract says the study varies geo-location while controlling other influencing factors, which matters because otherwise a difference between two result pages could be blamed on the wrong cause. A second difficulty is judgment. Bias is not visible by counting links alone. Two lists may contain different sources, different frames, or different regional emphases. On controversial topics, there is also no single neutral angle that everyone accepts. The paper therefore needs a way to judge results across multiple perspectives, at a scale large enough to cover engines, locations, topics, and time.
957.naive: A smart beginner might search the same controversial query from several cities, take screenshots, and compare the first few links by hand. That would show that results differ, but it would not prove a filter bubble. The differences might come from normal freshness, random ranking changes, language settings, or search-engine-specific behavior unrelated to location. The beginner might also ask one annotator to label whether a result is biased. That fails because controversial news is perspective-dependent: one reader may see regional relevance, another may see viewpoint narrowing. A single judge turns the evaluator's own assumptions into the measuring stick. The paper moves beyond this by controlling other factors, repeating observations over two months, comparing two engines, and using multiple LLM-represented perspectives for annotation.
957.ap: The central move is to treat a search result page as observable evidence of how an engine filters the world for a user in a place. The study fixes the topic and other search conditions, changes the geo-location, and then watches how the result lists differ. It does this across two major search engines, six controversial topics, and a two-month window. Then it uses large language models as scalable annotators standing in for multiple distinct perspectives. In plain terms, the model is asked to read search results through more than one viewpoint, so the analysis is not only asking whether two lists contain the same URLs. It is asking whether the lists present different regional or perspectival versions of the topic. The four research questions organize the comparison by engine, location, time, and topic.
957.mech: The mechanism starts with a controlled search setup. The input is a set of controversial topics and a set of geo-locations. For each topic, the system gathers search results from two globally dominant search engines while holding other influences fixed as much as the study design allows. That creates paired or grouped result lists where location is the main intended difference. The next layer compares those lists along several axes. Engine comparison asks whether one search engine's personalization behavior creates stronger or differently shaped bubbles than another. Location comparison asks whether result lists from different places reflect regional characteristics. Time comparison repeats the measurement over two months, so the study can observe whether bubbles shift after regional social events. Topic comparison asks whether every controversial issue behaves the same way or whether some topics produce sharper location-dependent separation. Annotation then adds meaning to the raw pages. Large language models, representing multiple distinct perspectives, label or judge the results so the study can estimate not just document overlap but the viewpoint structure of what was shown. The output is evidence about filter bubble formation patterns: which engine, which location, which time period, and which topic condition is associated with different result-page perspectives.
957.math: The main mathematical idea is controlled comparison. In ordinary language, that means changing one suspected cause while trying to keep other possible causes still. Here the suspected cause is geo-location. If the same topic searched under similar conditions produces different result patterns when the location changes, the study gains evidence that location is part of the explanation. A second idea is measurement of difference between ranked lists. A search page is ordered: higher positions matter more because users see them first. Even when the abstract does not name a specific ranking measure, the problem naturally requires comparing which sources and perspectives appear, where they appear, and how consistently they appear across locations and engines. A third idea is perspective annotation. Instead of treating bias as a hidden feeling, the study turns viewpoint judgments into repeated labels that can be counted and compared. Large language models act as scalable labeling instruments for multiple perspectives. The tradeoff is scale versus judgment reliability: automated annotations make many comparisons possible, but their conclusions depend on whether the model perspectives are well defined and stable. The fourth idea is temporal comparison, where repeated observations over two months let the study distinguish a fixed regional pattern from one that changes with events.
957.dots: This paper sits in Information Retrieval & Search because it studies the ranked list that a search engine returns, not only the documents themselves. It also belongs near Fairness, Bias & Responsible AI: the concern is unequal exposure to information, where a user's location may shape what evidence and viewpoints they receive. It connects to Misinformation & Trust because controversial news search is part of how people decide what is credible; if the visible evidence is locally narrowed, trust can fragment even when each individual result looks plausible. It also connects to evaluation papers that use LLM-based judges, such as repo entries about podcast search variability and search-system auditing. The shared problem is measurement at scale: human inspection is expensive, but raw counts miss meaning. This paper's specific version of that problem is measuring whether personalization turns geography into a hidden information boundary.
957.ww: The approach works better than simply noticing that search pages differ because it gives each difference a possible source. By varying geo-location while controlling other factors, the study reduces the chance that ordinary noise is mistaken for geographic bias. By comparing two engines, it can ask whether filter bubbles come from search in general or from particular personalization algorithms. By repeating the collection over two months, it can see whether a bubble is static or reacts to regional social events. That matters because news search is tied to time: a local event can legitimately change what is relevant, but it can also intensify a narrow local frame. The multi-perspective LLM annotation helps because filter bubbles are about meaning, not only about URL overlap. If two result pages show different sources but the same range of perspectives, the concern is weaker. If they show different perspectives in a systematic location-linked way, the evidence for a bubble is stronger. The design therefore aligns the measurement with the social failure being studied.
957.po: The payoff is an empirical way to describe geo-personalization bias in news search. According to the abstract, the study provides evidence for four kinds of formation patterns: different search engines contribute differently, user locations produce distinct regional bubbles, those bubbles evolve with regional social events over time, and topic characteristics affect how strongly bubbles form. The practical capability is an audit method for search engines that can scale across locations, topics, engines, and time without relying only on slow manual annotation. The public source code and scripts also make the study easier to inspect or repeat.
957.limits: The claims depend on the controls actually isolating geo-location from other influences such as timing, language, account state, device signals, and search-engine experiments. They also depend on the six controversial topics being representative enough to support broader claims about news search. LLM annotations are useful for scale, but they are not neutral measuring devices; their perspective labels must be well specified, and the abstract does not prove that they match diverse human judgments. The two-month window can show evolution, but not long-term effects on beliefs or behavior. The paper observes search results and inferred perspective patterns; it does not prove how individual users interpreted, clicked, trusted, or were changed by those results.

958.bp: This paper is about turning the public web into a disciplined source of trading ideas. Financial markets react to many written signals: regulatory filings, company disclosures, social media discussion, and other web material that investors may notice before prices fully settle. The practical problem is not simply reading more text. A trading desk or analyst needs a repeatable path from messy language to a hypothesis that can be tested: if this kind of event or statement appears, does a particular market action tend to follow? Traditionally, that path depends heavily on experts who choose what to read, decide what might matter, and design tests by hand. AutoHypo-Fin tries to automate the whole loop. It mines web data, turns extracted information into structured relationships, asks a language model to form candidate trading hypotheses using retrieved evidence, and then tests those hypotheses against historical market data before refining them.
958.wh: The hard part is that financial text is abundant, noisy, and easy to overinterpret. A regulatory filing may contain repeated boilerplate, a social media post may be rumor rather than evidence, and a true statement about a company may still have no useful trading consequence. Markets also punish slow reasoning: an idea that takes weeks to form may no longer be actionable. At the same time, speed alone is dangerous because a system can manufacture attractive-sounding stories that would have failed in past market conditions. The central tension is therefore between discovery and discipline. The system must search broadly enough to find ideas outside an expert's usual habits, but it must also force each idea through a test that asks whether the pattern has actually been associated with later returns, hit rate, and drawdown control. Without that testing loop, web-mined finance becomes story collection, not decision support.
958.naive: A smart beginner might collect financial news, filings, and social posts, ask a language model to summarize what looks important, and then let an analyst turn those summaries into trades. That sounds useful because it reduces reading time. It fails because summaries are not hypotheses. They do not specify the trigger, the expected market response, the assets involved, the holding rule, or the risk that the trade can lose heavily even when the story sounds right. Another beginner approach is to hand-code a few keyword rules, such as buying after positive filings or selling after negative social sentiment. That fails when language is indirect, context matters, and the same phrase can mean different things for different firms or market periods.
958.ap: The core idea is to make hypothesis generation a closed loop instead of a one-time act of inspiration. AutoHypo-Fin first extracts pieces of information from unstructured web sources, then organizes those pieces as a knowledge graph: a structured map where entities such as companies, filings, events, claims, and market concepts can be linked rather than left as loose text. When the system needs to generate a trading hypothesis, it does not ask a language model to invent from memory. It retrieves relevant evidence from that structured and textual store, uses the retrieved material to propose a candidate strategy, and then backtests the candidate on historical data. Backtesting acts as a reality check. Optimization then adjusts the strategy or selection process toward better measured behavior, such as stronger risk-adjusted returns, better hit rate, and lower drawdown.
958.mech: The mechanism starts with web-mined financial data: regulatory filings, social media, and other unstructured sources named in the abstract. The first transformation is information extraction. Instead of keeping every sentence as raw text, the system identifies usable pieces: entities, events, claims, relationships, and signals that might matter for markets. The second transformation is graph construction. The extracted pieces are placed into a knowledge graph, which means the system can follow links among companies, events, sources, and market-relevant concepts rather than treating each document as an isolated blob. The third step is retrieval-guided generation. For a proposed question or opportunity, the system retrieves relevant evidence and feeds it to a generator so the produced hypothesis is anchored in observed web material. The output at this point is a candidate trading strategy, not merely a prose explanation. The fourth step is backtesting: the candidate is run against historical market data from past years, including the 2019 to 2024 experimental period reported in the abstract. The system measures outcomes such as risk-adjusted return, hit rate, and drawdown. Finally, optimization uses those measurements as feedback, preferring and refining strategies that score better under the chosen financial criteria.
958.math: Several mathematical ideas are doing ordinary but important jobs here. Information extraction is a sorting and labeling problem: from a stream of words, the system must decide which spans refer to market-relevant things and which relationships connect them. A knowledge graph is graph reasoning: each node is a thing such as a company, filing, event, or concept, and each link says that two things are related in a specific way. The bet is that useful evidence can travel along those links, while unrelated text should not have equal influence. Retrieval is similarity and ranking: given a need, the system chooses a small set of relevant evidence from a much larger pile, deciding which differences matter enough to move an item up or down. Generation turns retrieved evidence into a proposed rule or strategy, but the mathematical discipline comes from backtesting and optimization. Backtesting estimates how a rule would have behaved across repeated historical cases. Optimization means defining what counts as better, such as more return per unit of risk and smaller drawdowns, then changing controllable strategy choices to improve that score. The tradeoff is discovery versus overfitting: a strategy can be tuned to past data too closely and still fail later.
958.dots: This paper connects several recurring conference ideas that often appear under different names. It is a retrieval paper because it must select relevant evidence from a huge web-mined collection. It is a knowledge graph paper because it treats financial facts as linked objects, not just separate documents. It is also an agent and tool-use paper in spirit because the system chains tools: extraction, graph construction, retrieval, generation, testing, and refinement. The repo's current data places nearby finance work around related pressures: financial asset recommendation ranks assets under user risk tolerance, financial fraud simulation builds testable financial scenarios when real data is hard to share, and Japanese financial text evaluation asks whether text representations work in a specialized financial language setting. The common thread is that finance does not reward fluent text alone. The model's output has to survive a downstream economic test, whether that test is return, risk, fraud detectability, or retrieval usefulness.
958.ww: The mechanism should help because it separates jobs that are easy to confuse. Raw web data is good for breadth, but bad for trust; information extraction narrows it to candidate facts. A knowledge graph is good for structure, but does not by itself say what trade to make; retrieval chooses the evidence most relevant to a particular hypothesis. A language model is good at forming coherent candidate ideas, but it can be persuasive without being true; backtesting forces the candidate into historical cases where losses, wins, and drawdowns can be measured. Optimization then gives the loop memory: strategies that perform badly under the chosen criteria should be refined or rejected, while strategies with better risk-adjusted behavior become preferred. This is stronger than the naive expert-only or summary-only approach because it makes every step produce an inspectable object: extracted facts, linked evidence, retrieved support, candidate strategy, historical test result, and refined strategy. The claimed improvements follow from this division of labor, not from any single component being magical.
958.po: The payoff is an automated pipeline for generating and testing financial hypotheses at web scale. The abstract reports experiments over 2019 to 2024 and says AutoHypo-Fin outperforms traditional strategies on risk-adjusted returns, hit rate, and drawdown control. In practical terms, the system buys speed and repeatability. Instead of relying only on experts to notice a web signal, translate it into a rule, and test it manually, the framework can generate, backtest, and refine candidate trading strategies as part of one loop. The ablation claim also matters: the abstract says each component contributes, suggesting the benefit comes from the full chain rather than a decorative add-on.
958.limits: The abstract leaves several assumptions open. The approach depends on extraction quality: if the system pulls wrong entities or relationships from filings and social media, the graph can organize false evidence neatly. It depends on retrieval quality: if the retrieved material is incomplete or biased toward loud sources, generation starts from a distorted view. It depends on backtests being honest proxies for future trading, which is always uncertain because markets change and past patterns can vanish once acted on. Optimization can also overfit to the 2019 to 2024 period if strategy choices are repeatedly adjusted to historical quirks. The abstract reports better risk-adjusted returns, hit rate, and drawdown, but it does not prove live trading performance, transaction-cost realism, or resistance to manipulated web signals.

959.bp: Yupp is about a common new decision: a person asks an AI system for help, but there is no single obvious model to trust. One model may be concise, another may be more cautious, another may be more creative, and another may notice a different angle. The product described in this paper turns that uncertainty into the main interface. Instead of hiding model choice behind one answer, it shows responses from multiple AI models side by side, so the user can compare perspectives at the moment of use. The deeper problem is not only answer generation. It is the measurement of model usefulness in ordinary situations, where people ask messy questions and judge answers by many qualities at once. The paper positions Yupp as both a consumer product and a data-gathering system: users get multiple perspectives, while their preferences become evidence for ranking models along different dimensions.
959.wh: The hard part is that model quality is not one thing. A fixed test set can ask whether a model gets known questions right, but a real user may care about tone, usefulness, novelty, caution, brevity, or whether the answer fits the situation. Those judgments are partly personal and partly task-dependent. If Yupp simply declared one winner, it would flatten many kinds of preference into one score. If it only showed many answers without collecting feedback, it would help one user in one moment but would not learn which models people value over time. The paper also has a product tension: feedback must be easy enough that people actually give it, yet structured enough to support leaderboards. The abstract says Yupp uses incentive mechanisms to encourage preference feedback, which matters because unpaid, unprompted feedback is often sparse and biased toward unusually strong reactions.
959.naive: A smart beginner might build a chat page with a dropdown: choose one model, ask a question, and maybe let users rate the answer with a star. That fails because the user cannot easily see what they missed. A five-star rating of one answer says little unless the user has seen plausible alternatives. Another beginner might run a private evaluation on prepared questions and publish a best-model list. That also misses the paper's target, because fixed datasets do not capture the informal judgments the abstract calls vibes from diverse populations. The simple approaches either remove comparison, remove real users, or reduce all quality to one average number.
959.ap: The core move is to make comparison the basic unit of interaction. Yupp sends the user's prompt to multiple AI models and presents the responses side by side. The user is then invited, through incentives, to say which response they prefer. That preference is not treated as a private note only for that session. It is gathered with many other user choices and turned into leaderboards that rank models along many dimensions. This changes model evaluation from a lab-only exercise into a living consumer loop: people get practical value from seeing several answers, and the platform receives paired judgments about which answer worked better for which kind of request. The paper also looks forward to a richer setting where AIs do not merely answer in parallel but collaborate and compete in multi-party dialogues.
959.mech: The mechanism starts with a user question or task. Yupp copies that same input to several AI models, so each model faces the same request. Each model returns an answer, and the product lays those answers out side by side. At this stage, the system has created a controlled comparison: the prompt is held constant, while the responding model changes. The user reads the options and expresses a preference, likely choosing the answer that best fits their need. The abstract does not specify every incentive, but it states that incentive mechanisms are used to encourage this feedback, so the product must turn feedback from an optional afterthought into a regular part of use. Then Yupp aggregates many such choices. Aggregation means counting and combining individual preference signals so that no single vote defines the result. Those combined signals feed leaderboards. A leaderboard is an ordered list, but here the order is not only one global ranking. The abstract says models are ranked along many dimensions, so the system likely separates different qualities instead of pretending that all questions share the same definition of better. The output is therefore twofold: the immediate user receives multiple perspectives, and the platform produces public or internal rankings that summarize how diverse users prefer different models in real use.
959.math: The main mathematics is ranking from comparisons. A comparison is simpler than an absolute score: given two or more answers to the same prompt, the user says which one they prefer. Repeated many times, these local choices can be combined into an ordered view of models. The plain idea is like sorting a pile of objects by repeatedly asking, which of these two belongs higher? The hard part is that users, prompts, and judging dimensions differ. Probability is therefore involved in the everyday sense of estimating uncertain chances from repeated observations: after many choices, the system can estimate that one model is more likely to be preferred for a certain kind of need, while still leaving room for uncertainty. Aggregation is another mathematical idea: many noisy individual judgments are combined so the final signal is less dependent on one person's mood or one strange prompt. Incentives matter because the measurements are created by people, not by passive sensors. If incentives change who responds or why they respond, they also change the data being aggregated. The central tradeoff is personalization versus public comparison: a leaderboard needs shared order, while real preference may depend on the person and task.
959.dots: This paper connects to ranking because its leaderboards turn many user choices into ordered model lists. It connects to recommendation because Yupp is implicitly helping users choose which AI model or answer fits their current need. It connects to evaluation of language models because it argues that fixed test datasets are not enough; the product gathers real-use judgments from diverse populations. It also touches the conference's broader interest in multi-agent and tool-use systems. Neighboring papers in the repo's LLM agents and tool-use family ask how language models should choose tools, share work, or act in production settings. Yupp studies a related surface: how multiple models can be placed in front of a person, compared fairly enough to be useful, and eventually made to collaborate or compete in dialogue. The shared problem is controlled choice among many intelligent systems under uncertain human preference.
959.ww: The approach works when comparison reveals information that isolated use hides. If a user sees only one answer, they may accept it because it is fluent, even if another model would have offered a clearer warning or a more useful structure. Side-by-side display makes differences visible at the exact moment the user can judge them. The same prompt gives each model a common starting point, so the user's preference is more informative than a rating collected from unrelated questions. Across many users, repeated preferences can expose patterns that a fixed lab test would miss: one model may win on explanation, another on creative range, another on practical directness. Incentives help because the platform needs enough feedback to make aggregation meaningful. The consumer benefit and the measurement benefit support each other: users participate because comparison helps them now, and their choices help build rankings that guide future users and model builders.
959.po: The payoff is a platform where users do not have to bet on a single AI answer. They can consult several models at once, compare perspectives, and express which response they prefer. In return, Yupp turns scattered user judgments into leaderboards across many dimensions, giving a real-use counterpart to fixed model tests. The abstract also frames the product as a bridge from research lab ideas into an engaging consumer experience. Looking ahead, the same setting could support multi-party AI dialogues where models collaborate and compete, not just answer separately.
959.limits: The abstract leaves important questions open. It does not specify the incentive mechanisms, the dimensions used in the leaderboards, or how the system corrects for users who give careless, strategic, or highly idiosyncratic feedback. The approach assumes that side-by-side preferences are meaningful evidence of model quality, but preferences can reflect style, familiarity, or presentation order rather than better reasoning. Aggregation helps only if the collected population is diverse enough for the claimed real-world signal. The paper also envisions multi-party AI dialogues, but the abstract does not prove that collaboration among models will produce better or safer answers than parallel comparison.
